mean: to make a decision promptly on the spot
lit: facing the critical moment, decide at once

use.how: A verb phrase, often after 必须, 要 or 他 as predicate: 关键时刻他当机立断。 Praises a quick, decisive call at a critical moment.

near.diff: 毫不犹豫 describes doing anything without hesitation; 当机立断 is specifically making a decisive call at a critical, urgent moment.

cue: A fire breaks out in the warehouse, and the manager immediately orders everyone out and calls for help without waiting for head office. How do you praise her?

ctx.s: 情况紧急，你必须{当机立断}。
ctx.en: It's an emergency; you have to decide right now.

ctx.s: 会议讨论了半天也没有结果，最后总经理{当机立断}，拍板定了方案。
ctx.en: The meeting went round in circles for ages; in the end the general manager made the call on the spot and settled the plan.

ctx.s: 多亏经理{当机立断}，公司才避免了更大的损失。
ctx.en: Thanks to the manager's quick decision, the company avoided an even bigger loss.

ctx.s: “还等什么？{当机立断}吧，马上把病人送医院！”
ctx.en: "What are you waiting for? Make the call: get the patient to hospital now!"

ctx.s: 面对突如其来的暴雨，船长{当机立断}，下令返航。
ctx.en: Faced with the sudden storm, the captain decided on the spot and ordered the ship back to port.

ctx.s: 做生意有时候需要{当机立断}，犹豫太久就会错过机会。
ctx.en: In business you sometimes have to decide on the spot; hesitate too long and you miss the chance.

bad.s: 我想了三个月，终于{当机立断}买了这辆车。
bad.en: (meant: after three months of thinking I finally decided to buy the car)
bad.why: It means deciding instantly at a critical moment; three months of thought is the opposite.

bad.s: 他是一个{当机立断}。
bad.en: (meant: he is a decisive person)
bad.why: It is a verb phrase describing an action, not a noun for a kind of person; to call someone decisive use a plain adjective instead.

use.how: An adjective for a person's character: 他太优柔寡断了; also 优柔寡断的性格. Criticises someone who habitually cannot make decisions.

near.diff: 犹豫不决 is being unable to decide in one particular case; 优柔寡断 is a lasting weakness of character.

cue: Your friend takes weeks to pick a restaurant, a phone or a job offer, and always ends up missing out. What flaw of character do you point out?

ctx.s: 他什么都好，就是有点{优柔寡断}。
ctx.en: He's great in every way, except he's a bit indecisive.

ctx.s: 你这种{优柔寡断}的性格得改一改，不然总会错过机会。
ctx.en: You need to change that indecisive nature of yours, or you'll keep missing your chances.

ctx.s: 一个{优柔寡断}的人，很难当好领导。
ctx.en: Someone who is irresolute by nature will find it hard to be a good leader.

ctx.s: 她知道自己性格{优柔寡断}，所以很羡慕做事果断的人。
ctx.en: She knows she's indecisive by nature, so she really admires people who act decisively.

ctx.s: “你为什么不早点拒绝他？”“唉，都怪我太{优柔寡断}。”
ctx.en: "Why didn't you turn him down sooner?" "Sigh, it's because I'm far too indecisive."

ctx.s: 小说的主人公{优柔寡断}，一次次错过了心爱的人。
ctx.en: The novel's hero is irresolute and misses the woman he loves time after time.

bad.s: 这位老师说话{优柔寡断}，学生们都很喜欢她。
bad.en: (meant: this teacher speaks gently, and the students love her)
bad.why: The idiom criticises a habit of indecision; it cannot be used to praise someone's soft, gentle way of speaking.

bad.s: 今天的天气{优柔寡断}，一会儿晴一会儿雨。
bad.en: (meant: the weather is changeable today)
bad.why: It describes a person's character in making decisions; weather cannot be indecisive.

lit: to chop through nails and cut iron

use.how: Usually adverbial with 地 before 说, 回答 or 拒绝: 他斩钉截铁地说。 Describes speech or an attitude that is firm and leaves no room for doubt.

near.diff: 一言为定 seals an agreement between two people; 斩钉截铁 describes the firm, uncompromising way one person says something.

cue: Asked whether he would ever sell his late father's shop, the son answered at once and in a tone that left no doubt: never. How did he answer?

ctx.s: 他{斩钉截铁}地说：“不行！”
ctx.en: He said flatly: "No way!"

ctx.s: 我问她会不会回来，她{斩钉截铁}地回答：“不会。”
ctx.en: I asked if she'd come back, and she answered firmly: "No."

ctx.s: 面对对方的高价收购，老板{斩钉截铁}地拒绝了。
ctx.en: Faced with the other side's high buyout offer, the owner turned it down flat.

ctx.s: 她的语气{斩钉截铁}，谁也不敢再劝她。
ctx.en: Her tone was so firm that no one dared try to talk her round again.

ctx.s: “你确定是他吗？”“我能{斩钉截铁}地告诉你，就是他。”
ctx.en: "Are you sure it was him?" "I can tell you with absolute certainty: it was him."

ctx.s: 记者追问此事，发言人{斩钉截铁}地否认了所有传闻。
ctx.en: When reporters pressed the matter, the spokesperson flatly denied all the rumours.

bad.s: 工人们正在工地上{斩钉截铁}，非常辛苦。
bad.en: (meant: the workers are cutting metal on the building site)
bad.why: It is only a figure for firm speech or attitude, never a literal description of cutting metal.

bad.s: 他犹豫了半天，最后{斩钉截铁}地说：“也许吧。”
bad.en: (meant: after hesitating he finally said, 'maybe')
bad.why: A hesitant 'maybe' is the opposite of a firm reply; the idiom needs a clear, definite statement.

lit: three in the morning, four in the evening

story.text: A man who kept monkeys had to cut their food, so he told them they would get three nuts in the morning and four in the evening. The monkeys were furious. He then offered four in the morning and three in the evening, and they were delighted, though the total was the same. The fable first mocked people fooled by an empty change of words; today the phrase is used for someone who keeps changing their mind or loyalties.
story.source: 《庄子·齐物论》, also in 《列子·黄帝》

use.how: Predicate or attributive: 他做事朝三暮四; 朝三暮四的人. Criticises someone who keeps switching plans, jobs, partners or loyalties.

near.diff: 三心二意 is not putting one's whole mind into what one is doing now; 朝三暮四 is repeatedly switching from one choice or loyalty to another.
出尔反尔 is going back on a specific promise; 朝三暮四 is a general habit of changing one's mind or attachments.

cue: Your cousin has changed his university major three times in two years and now wants to switch again. How do you criticise this habit?

ctx.s: 你不能这样{朝三暮四}，选定了就要坚持。
ctx.en: You can't keep changing your mind like this; once you've chosen, stick with it.

ctx.s: 他今天想学画画，明天想学钢琴，总是{朝三暮四}的。
ctx.en: Today he wants to learn painting, tomorrow piano; he's always flitting from one thing to another.

ctx.s: 她不喜欢{朝三暮四}的男人，只想找个踏实的人。
ctx.en: She doesn't like fickle men; she just wants someone steady and reliable.

ctx.s: 老板最怕员工{朝三暮四}，干几个月就跳槽。
ctx.en: What bosses fear most is fickle staff who job-hop after a few months.

ctx.s: “这次你真的不会再改主意了吧？”“放心，我不是{朝三暮四}的人。”
ctx.en: "You really won't change your mind again this time?" "Don't worry, I'm not the fickle type."

ctx.s: 他在感情上{朝三暮四}，朋友们都不敢把人介绍给他。
ctx.en: He's so fickle in love that his friends don't dare introduce anyone to him.

bad.s: 这个城市的天气{朝三暮四}，早上冷晚上热。
bad.en: (meant: the weather in this city is changeable)
bad.why: It criticises a person's fickle choices or loyalties; changeable weather needs a different expression.

bad.s: 他每天{朝三暮四}地工作，从早忙到晚。
bad.en: (meant: he works from morning to night every day)
bad.why: The numbers and times are not about working hours; it means fickle, not busy all day.

mean: changing from one moment to the next
lit: in the space of a blink and a breath, ten thousand changes

use.how: Predicate or attributive, of situations, markets, weather or battles: 市场瞬息万变; 瞬息万变的局势. Stresses speed and unpredictability of change.

near.diff: 日新月异 is steady progress seen over days and months, and is positive; 瞬息万变 is rapid, unpredictable change from moment to moment.
千变万化 stresses the endless variety of forms; 瞬息万变 stresses how fast things change.

cue: A stock trader explains why she can't leave her screen even for a coffee: prices could swing in either direction any second. How does she describe the market?

ctx.s: 股市{瞬息万变}，谁也说不准明天会怎样。
ctx.en: The stock market changes by the second; nobody can say what tomorrow will bring.

ctx.s: 山里的天气{瞬息万变}，出发前一定要带好雨衣。
ctx.en: Mountain weather changes in an instant, so be sure to bring a raincoat before you set off.

ctx.s: 面对{瞬息万变}的病情，医生必须随时做好抢救准备。
ctx.en: Faced with a patient's condition that can change at any moment, the doctors must be ready to intervene at all times.

ctx.s: 比赛场上局势{瞬息万变}，最后一分钟还可能被翻盘。
ctx.en: On the pitch the situation changes in a flash; a lead can be overturned even in the final minute.

ctx.s: 战场上形势{瞬息万变}，指挥官必须随时调整计划。
ctx.en: On the battlefield things change from moment to moment, and the commander must adjust plans constantly.

ctx.s: 网络舆论{瞬息万变}，昨天的热点今天就没人提了。
ctx.en: Online opinion shifts by the minute; yesterday's hot topic is forgotten today.

bad.s: 十年过去了，家乡的面貌{瞬息万变}，到处都是新楼。
bad.en: (meant: over ten years my hometown has changed greatly)
bad.why: Change spread over years is described with idioms of steady progress; this one is for change happening moment by moment.

bad.s: 他的发型{瞬息万变}，变得很好看。
bad.en: (meant: his hairstyle changed a lot and looks great now)
bad.why: It describes a fast-shifting, unpredictable situation, not a single change in someone's look.

lit: to shed the mortal womb and exchange one's bones

story.text: The phrase began as a Daoist term. A person who cultivated the Way successfully was said to shed the body they were born with and exchange ordinary human bones for the bones of an immortal. Later it came to mean any complete change of a person or thing, especially a change for the better.

use.how: Predicate or after 发生了/经历了 ... 的变化: 他像是脱胎换骨了。 Said of a person, team or organisation changed completely, usually for the better.

near.diff: 焕然一新 is about looking brand new on the surface (a room, a street); 脱胎换骨 is a change to the very nature of a person or organisation.
面目全非 is changed beyond recognition, usually for the worse; 脱胎换骨 is a deep change, usually for the better.

cue: A lazy, rude student came back from a year of military service disciplined, polite and hard-working, a completely different person. How do his teachers describe him?

ctx.s: 当了两年兵，他像{脱胎换骨}了一样。
ctx.en: After two years in the army he seems like a completely new person.

ctx.s: 新教练来了以后，这支球队{脱胎换骨}，连赢了好几场。
ctx.en: After the new coach arrived, the team was utterly transformed and won several games in a row.

ctx.s: 经过这次改革，这家老工厂发生了{脱胎换骨}的变化。
ctx.en: After this reform, the old factory went through a complete transformation.

ctx.s: “你最近变化好大啊！”“是啊，生了一场大病，我感觉自己{脱胎换骨}了。”
ctx.en: "You've changed so much lately!" "Yes, after a serious illness I feel like a different person."

ctx.s: 要想{脱胎换骨}，光改几个坏习惯是不够的。
ctx.en: If you want to transform yourself completely, just changing a few bad habits isn't enough.

ctx.s: 这款手机的新版本几乎{脱胎换骨}，跟旧款完全不一样。
ctx.en: The new version of this phone is practically reinvented; it's nothing like the old model.

bad.s: 她剪了短发，{脱胎换骨}了。
bad.en: (meant: she cut her hair short and looks different)
bad.why: A new haircut is a surface change; the idiom means a change to someone's whole character or nature.

bad.s: 他出了车祸，身体{脱胎换骨}，再也不能走路了。
bad.en: (meant: after the accident his body was badly damaged)
bad.why: Despite the word for bone, it has nothing to do with injury; it means a thorough, usually positive transformation.

lit: each time, the state of things sinks lower

story.text: Asked where the Way could be found, Zhuangzi named ants, weeds, tiles and even dung. He explained with an image from the market: to judge how fat a pig is, you press lower and lower down its leg, and the lower you press, the clearer it becomes. His wording was 'each time lower, the more evident'. Later writers reversed the words into today's form, meaning that things keep getting worse.

use.how: A predicate after a subject such as 身体, 生意, 成绩, 经济: 他的身体每况愈下。 Describes a gradual, continuing decline.

near.diff: 一落千丈 is a sudden, steep fall; 每况愈下 is a gradual decline that keeps getting worse.

cue: Year after year, the old bookshop sold fewer books, cut staff, then hours, and now struggles to pay rent. How do you describe its business?

ctx.s: 爷爷年纪大了，身体{每况愈下}。
ctx.en: Grandpa is getting old and his health is going from bad to worse.

ctx.s: 自从附近开了大超市，这家小店的生意就{每况愈下}。
ctx.en: Ever since a big supermarket opened nearby, this little shop's business has gone steadily downhill.

ctx.s: 他上了高中以后迷上游戏，成绩{每况愈下}。
ctx.en: After starting high school he got hooked on games, and his grades kept slipping.

ctx.s: “这家餐厅最近怎么样？”“服务{每况愈下}，我都不想去了。”
ctx.en: "How's that restaurant these days?" "The service keeps getting worse; I don't even want to go anymore."

ctx.s: 这位作家后期的作品质量{每况愈下}，读者越来越少。
ctx.en: The quality of the writer's later works declined steadily, and he had fewer and fewer readers.

ctx.s: 由于长期污染，这条河的水质{每况愈下}。
ctx.en: Because of long-term pollution, the river's water quality has been getting steadily worse.

bad.s: 经过治疗，他的病情{每况愈下}，很快就出院了。
bad.en: (meant: after treatment his condition improved and he was soon discharged)
bad.why: It means getting worse and worse, never better.

bad.s: 他从楼梯上{每况愈下}，摔伤了腿。
bad.en: (meant: he fell down the stairs)
bad.why: It is about a situation declining over time, not physically going down or falling.

mean: seen so often it is no longer news
lit: seen again and again, no longer fresh

story.text: The Han official Lu Jia divided his wealth among his five sons and planned to travel, staying with each son in turn. With visits elsewhere, he said, he would come to each of them only two or three times a year, because a guest who comes too often no longer gets fresh food prepared for him, and he did not want to burden them. His wording used a different first character; the present form came later.
story.source: 《史记·郦生陆贾列传》 (as 数见不鲜)

use.how: A predicate after a phenomenon, often with 已经 or 早就: 这种骗局已经屡见不鲜。 Said of things, often problems, that happen so often they no longer surprise anyone.

near.diff: 家常便饭 is colloquial and says something is routine in one's own life (加班是家常便饭); 屡见不鲜 is more written and describes a phenomenon in society.
习以为常 is about a person being used to something; 屡见不鲜 is about the thing being common.

cue: A journalist writes that fake online reviews used to cause outrage, but now they appear so often that nobody is shocked any more. What does she say about them?

ctx.s: 这种电话诈骗现在已经{屡见不鲜}了。
ctx.en: This kind of phone scam is so common now that it's nothing new.

ctx.s: 在大城市，堵车早就{屡见不鲜}，没人会觉得奇怪。
ctx.en: In big cities traffic jams are an everyday sight; nobody finds them strange.

ctx.s: 名人在网上发错消息的事{屡见不鲜}。
ctx.en: Celebrities posting the wrong thing online is nothing new.

ctx.s: “又有人插队了！”“这种事{屡见不鲜}，别生气了。”
ctx.en: "Someone's cut in line again!" "That happens all the time; don't get upset."

ctx.s: 十年前无人驾驶汽车还很新奇，如今在一些城市已经{屡见不鲜}。
ctx.en: Ten years ago driverless cars were a novelty; now in some cities they're a common sight.

ctx.s: 这类新闻{屡见不鲜}，说明问题还没有得到真正解决。
ctx.en: Stories like this come up again and again, which shows the problem has not really been solved.

bad.s: 这道菜{屡见不鲜}，不太新鲜了，别吃了。
bad.en: (meant: this dish isn't fresh any more, don't eat it)
bad.why: The 'fresh' in it means novel, not freshly made; it says a phenomenon is common, not that food has gone off.

bad.s: 我{屡见不鲜}他，所以不想再见他了。
bad.en: (meant: I've seen him so often I don't want to see him again)
bad.why: It cannot take a person as an object; it is a predicate saying that a kind of event is common.

mean: emerging one after another without end
lit: appearing layer upon layer, never exhausted

use.how: A predicate after things that keep appearing: 新产品层出不穷; 问题层出不穷. Stresses that new ones, often of new kinds, keep emerging.

near.diff: 络绎不绝 is people or vehicles arriving in a continuous stream; 层出不穷 is new things, ideas or problems constantly emerging.
接二连三 is events happening in quick succession; 层出不穷 stresses an endless supply of new ones, often over a longer period.

cue: Every few months there is a new app, a new gadget and a new online trend that nobody had heard of before. How do you describe these innovations?

ctx.s: 现在手机的新功能{层出不穷}。
ctx.en: New phone features keep appearing all the time.

ctx.s: 网络上的新词{层出不穷}，老年人常常看不懂。
ctx.en: New internet slang keeps popping up, and older people often can't follow it.

ctx.s: 这家公司创意{层出不穷}，每年都有新产品上市。
ctx.en: This company has an endless stream of ideas and launches new products every year.

ctx.s: 这套系统用了三年，各种新问题还是{层出不穷}。
ctx.en: This system has been in use for three years, and new kinds of problems still keep cropping up.

ctx.s: “诈骗手段怎么这么多？”“是啊，新花样{层出不穷}，防不胜防。”
ctx.en: "Why are there so many scam tricks?" "I know, new ones keep appearing; you can't guard against them all."

ctx.s: 随着科技发展，各种新职业{层出不穷}。
ctx.en: As technology develops, all kinds of new professions keep emerging.

bad.s: 春节期间，商场里的顾客{层出不穷}。
bad.en: (meant: during Spring Festival customers kept streaming into the mall)
bad.why: For customers streaming in, use the idiom for a steady flow of arrivals; this one is for new things or phenomena emerging.

bad.s: 他的钱{层出不穷}，花也花不完。
bad.en: (meant: he has so much money it never runs out)
bad.why: It is about new kinds of things constantly appearing, not about an amount of money that never runs out.

mean: arriving in a steady, unbroken stream
lit: linked one after another, never breaking off

use.how: A predicate after people, visitors or vehicles: 游客络绎不绝; 来参观的人络绎不绝. Describes a continuous flow of arrivals, never things or ideas.

near.diff: 人山人海 is a huge crowd gathered in one place at one time; 络绎不绝 is people coming one group after another without a break.
层出不穷 is new things or problems constantly emerging; 络绎不绝 is a steady stream of people or vehicles arriving.

cue: From opening time to closing time, visitors keep arriving at the new museum, group after group, never a quiet moment. How do you describe them?

ctx.s: 博物馆一开门，游客就{络绎不绝}。
ctx.en: As soon as the museum opened, visitors came in a steady stream.

ctx.s: 新店开张那天，来祝贺的朋友{络绎不绝}。
ctx.en: On the day the new shop opened, friends came to congratulate them one after another all day.

ctx.s: 国庆期间，前往景区的车辆{络绎不绝}。
ctx.en: During the National Day holiday, cars kept streaming towards the scenic spot.

ctx.s: “你们医院每天都这么忙吗？”“是啊，看病的人从早到晚{络绎不绝}。”
ctx.en: "Is your hospital this busy every day?" "Yes, patients keep coming from morning till night."

ctx.s: 这位老画家去世后，前来悼念的人{络绎不绝}。
ctx.en: After the old painter died, people came to pay their respects in an unbroken stream.

ctx.s: 山顶的寺庙香火很旺，上山的人{络绎不绝}。
ctx.en: The temple on the summit is very popular, and people climb the mountain in a continuous stream.

bad.s: 最近公司的问题{络绎不绝}，老板很头疼。
bad.en: (meant: problems at the company keep coming up)
bad.why: It describes people or vehicles arriving in a stream; problems that keep emerging take a different idiom.

bad.s: 他说话{络绎不绝}，一个小时都没停。
bad.en: (meant: he talked non-stop for an hour)
bad.why: It is about a stream of arrivals, not about one person talking without pause; that needs a different idiom.
